Fair. Plain words from here on, and I'll say nothing more about that branch.

**What I meant by a fact.** Something that is already true in the app at that moment, that the app knows, and that the model would need to be told. Three examples from the catalogue:

- OrcaSlicer refused to slice, and the reason it gave. Today the model is told only "it did not finish". The reason is sitting in the app, in the same record that draws the print-issue chip on the canvas. Passing it through means the model can say "OrcaSlicer refused because PETG cannot go on the Cool Plate" instead of guessing.
- When the model records what the print is for, what the printer, filament and process presets currently are, and whether the purpose changed from what was recorded before. The app knows all of that. Saying it in the tool's reply at that moment is what gets the model to check the presets then, which is the behaviour you most want.
- After the person restores an older version of the project, whether the plan the model wrote earlier still applies. The app knows the plan went stale. The model is not told.

A fact goes into the reply the tool gives the model, or into the short description of the project that rides along with every message. It is not an instruction. It is information, so the model can reason from it. That is different from a skill, which is a page of English telling the model how to think about a situation. The catalogue's point was that most situations need a fact, and only the file-open moment needs a page of English.

**What I meant by a description move.** Every tool the model can call has a short description, the sentence or two that tells the model what the tool does. Two sentences in today's system prompt are really about one tool each, and they would move out of the system prompt into that tool's description:

- "If preparing takes several changes, record the plan with plan_set before applying them" is about one tool, plan_set. It would become part of plan_set's own description.
- "A material and its saved filament preset are separate choices" is about choosing presets. It would go into the descriptions of the tools that list and set presets.

The reason to move them: the system prompt is read on every message, including "what infill should I use". A tool's description is read when the model is deciding whether to call that tool, which is exactly when the sentence matters. And the printer chat, the filament chat and the external tools interface see the tool descriptions too, so the rule reaches them without being repeated.

**The whole picture in plain words.** The system prompt shrinks to principles. The print-preparation procedure comes out of it. In its place: three facts the app starts telling the model at the right moments, two sentences moved into the tool descriptions they belong to, and the existing file-open instructions kept as they are, with the plate picture added so the model can see the object. Then we measure the old prompt against the new one, one run per case.

The one thing that moves first, on its own, is the slice-refusal reason, because it fixes a failure that happens today regardless of any prompt change.

You’re right, and my earlier description was wrong on this point. Here is what the code actually does.
Without `wait` (the default): `slice_start` posts the same event Orca’s Slice button posts, and returns `started: true`, state `succeeded`, at once (ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp:1786). The adapter’s only checks before that are “no slice already running” and the plate’s `can_slice()` (OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:1759). Orca’s handler then runs `reslice()` → `update_background_process` → `validate`. When validation fails, Orca pushes a ValidateError notification, marks the plate invalid, and returns without starting anything (Plater.cpp:8075). None of that comes back to the tool. So the model is told the slice started when nothing happened. That is the “success with nothing sliced” from October 15.
With `wait: true`: the coordinator polls until “the run was seen running and has stopped”, or “the plate reads as sliced for 3 seconds”, or 15 minutes pass (ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp:837). A validation refusal never starts a run and never slices the plate, so the first two never fire. The call sits for 15 minutes and then returns `finished: false` with no reason. That is the “hang on retry”. Only a slice that starts and then dies mid-run (a real slicing error, which fires the completion event) ends the wait promptly with `finished: false`.
So “the result says it did not finish” was true only after a 15-minute wait. In practice the tool says success.
What this means for the fix. It is still a result field, but the refusal has to be detected at start, not only at end. Orca’s validation runs synchronously inside the Slice-button handler, so by the time `ProcessEvent` returns the app already knows: either a run is in flight (`is_background_process_slicing()` true), or the plate is already sliced and nothing needed doing, or the plate is now marked invalid and a ValidateError notification is held. In the third case the tool should return `started: false` right away, with the blockers from the issue monitor, instead of `started: true`. The same check lets the `wait` path exit immediately rather than at the 15-minute timeout. The 15-minute fallback then stays only for a run that genuinely never reports.
That also means the schema changes (`started` can be false on a succeeded call, plus a `blockers` field), so the eval recording must be re-made, and the description’s sentence “return once it has started” needs to say what happens when Orca refuses.
Why can't we just listen to those events As orchestriser report them? Why do we have to lump them either at the beginning or at the end?
We can, and the app already does half of it. The limit isn’t where we listen. It’s when the model can read.
What already listens. The workspace adapter is bound to Orca’s slice-status event and records, at the moment of the transition, why a slice was invalidated (OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:619). The coordinator subscribes to workspace changes (ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp:377). The issue monitor is bound to Orca’s completion event and to the notification list. So the events are reaching us. What nobody does is carry a refusal or failure into the workspace snapshot, and the slice wait polls conditions instead of ending on the event.
Why I said “beginning or end”. A tool call gets exactly one reply, and between making the call and getting the reply the model reads nothing. So however many events arrive, there are only two moments the model can learn about them: the reply to a call that is still open, or the next request, through the workspace block or a note. That’s a fact about how the model talks to us, not about Orca’s events. “Report as they happen” means: write the event into the snapshot the instant it arrives, and let whichever reading moment comes next pick it up.
What that looks like, event-driven:

1. The adapter also binds Orca’s completion event and watches for the ValidateError notification, and records per plate a `blocked` reason, the same way it records `invalidated_by` today: set at the transition, cleared when the plate slices. It publishes a `Slicing` change, which it already does for slice-state changes.
2. The snapshot carries that field. The slicing section of every tool result and the `<workspace>` block on every message then show `"blocked": "<Orca's words>"` for that plate, with no further plumbing, because both are built from the snapshot.
3. The coordinator’s existing subscription ends a waiting `slice_start` the moment a `blocked` reason appears for its plate, instead of waiting for the 15-minute timeout. The reply carries the reason because the slicing section does.
4. For a `slice_start` without `wait`, the reply has already gone, but the next workspace block shows `blocked`, and so does `slice_report`.

This is better than what I proposed before: one recording point, no seam from the issue monitor into the coordinator, and it covers a slice the person started from the Slice button too, which a check inside the tool never could. The one judgment call is which notification kinds count as “blocked” versus a warning. The issue monitor’s severity rule, blocker versus warning, already answers that and can be reused.
The slice finish is already event-driven, right?
Half of it is. The detection is event-driven; the finishing of the tool call is not.
Event-driven part. The adapter listens to Orca’s slice-status event and publishes a workspace change when a plate starts or stops being sliced. The coordinator subscribes to those changes and, in the subscription itself, keeps the two flags for the slice it started: `m_slice_seen_running` and `m_slice_ended` (ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp:377). So the coordinator learns that the run began and ended at the moment Orca says so.
Polled part. The waiting `slice_start` call is not finished inside that subscription. It is finished in `finish_slice_waits`, which runs from `pump()`, which `AgentHost::pump_tools` calls on the app’s periodic tick (AgentHost.cpp:1908). On each tick it re-derives the state from a fresh snapshot (`seen_running`, “all plates sliced for 3 seconds”, 15-minute cap) and only then writes the reply. Oddly, it keeps its own `seen_running` per wait rather than using the `m_slice_ended` flag the subscription already maintains, so the same fact is tracked twice.
Why that matters for the refusal. A validation refusal never flips `slicing.running`, so the slice-status event never fires and the subscription never sees a transition. Neither the event path nor the poll has anything to react to, and the poll runs out the 15-minute clock. The missing piece is not a listener for the end of a run; it is a listener for “Orca declined to start one”, which is a different Orca signal (the ValidateError notification, or the completion event with an error for a mid-run failure). Once the adapter records that into the snapshot and publishes a change, the existing subscription sees it, and the waiting call can be ended right there, in the callback, instead of on the next tick. That also removes the duplicated bookkeeping.
Any reason why it has to be a poll?
No hard reason. The poll covers three things, and none of them needs a poll.

1. “Orca did not need to slice.” If the plate is already sliced and nothing changed, Orca’s Slice button does nothing and no slice-status event fires, so a purely event-driven wait would never end. The poll handles it with the “plates read as sliced for 3 seconds” rule. But that case is knowable the instant `start_slice` returns: Orca’s `reslice()` runs synchronously inside the posted event, so when `ProcessEvent` comes back either a run is in flight, or the plate is still sliced and nothing started, or the plate is now marked invalid. Checking the snapshot right there decides it. No waiting.
2. The refusal. Same moment, same check, once the adapter records the ValidateError into the snapshot. Today the poll can’t see it at all and runs 15 minutes.
3. A run that never reports. The 15-minute cap. That is a timeout, and a timeout wants one timer, not a check on every tick.

The run that does start and end normally is already event-driven: the adapter publishes on the slice-status transition, and the coordinator’s subscription sees it (ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp:377). The only reason the reply isn’t written there is that the author chose to defer it to `pump()`. There is no re-entrancy barrier: `invalidate_pending`, called from that same subscription, already fails pending exports and notifies observers from inside the callback (ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp:2018).
So the shape without a poll is: decide the no-run and refused cases synchronously at start; finish the normal case in the subscription when `slicing.running` goes true then false for that plate; keep one timer for the never-reports case. The `SliceWait` map and its duplicate `seen_running` flag go away. The one thing to keep an eye on is that a reply written inside a workspace-change callback hands control to the agent host while the adapter is still mid-publish, which is the same situation `invalidate_pending` already creates, so it is a known-safe path rather than a new one.
